deep.reconstruction:
This page closes Chapter 1 (on the classification of numbers by how many prime factors they have) with three empirical remarks on the distribution of primes. It then opens Chapter 2, on divisors.

§52 (qualitative). Among small numbers primes are very frequent and composites rare. Further along, composites become more frequent and primes rarer. In modern terms: pi(x)/x decreases.

§53. The sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, ... shows no visible law from which it could be generated. Still, it is certain that primes thin out on the whole. Note that 1 is listed as a prime here, consistent with the previous page, where 1 was included among the 26 primes up to 100.

§54 (data from existing prime tables, by hundreds). With N(a,b) = number of primes in (a,b], the claims are:
- N(0,100) = 26, i.e. 25 primes plus the unit 1.
- N(100,200) = 21.
- N(200,300) = 16.
- N(400,500) = 17.
- N(1400,1500) = 17 ('totidemque').
- N(79700,79800) = 3.
- N(90000,90100) = 13.
The point is that the count per hundred does not decrease monotonically but fluctuates irregularly.

Checking 79700–79800 (my sieve):
- The candidates prime to 2, 3 and 5 were sieved by every prime up to 281, since sqrt(79800) ≈ 282.5.
- Most candidates fall to small primes.
- Three late eliminations: 79753 = 173·461, 79771 = 241·331, 79799 = 199·401.
- Survivors: 79757, 79769, 79777. This is exactly 3 primes, as Euler says.

Checking 1400–1500: the primes are 1409, 1423, 1427, 1429, 1433, 1439, 1447, 1451, 1453, 1459, 1471, 1481, 1483, 1487, 1489, 1493, 1499. That is 17.

Checking 90000–90100: from memory, the primes are 90001, 90007, 90011, 90017, 90019, 90023, 90031, 90053, 90059, 90067, 90071, 90073, 90089. That is 13; this list was not re-derived by sieving.

Caput II, De divisoribus numerorum.
- §55–56 (definitions): if N = n·a, then a is a divisor of N and n, the 'index of multiplicity', is the quotient. So N/a = n.
- §57: since multiplication is commutative, n is also a divisor, with quotient a. Divisor × quotient = N.
- §58–59: 1 | N with quotient N, and N | N with quotient 1.
- §60: d is a divisor of N if and only if N is a multiple of d (the trivial multiple 1·d included).
- §61: a prime p is a multiple of no number except 1 (and itself), so its divisors are exactly {1, p}.
- §62: primes therefore have exactly two divisors, while 1 has only one. For this reason 1 is usually not counted among the primes. This is a note on convention.
- §63: for a number of the second class, N = pq with p, q prime, the divisors are 1, p, q, pq. Distinct primes are tacitly assumed; the next page (§64) treats the case p = q separately (divisors 1, p, p²).
errors: No numerical errors found. Every century count checked is correct (79700–79800 by explicit sieve; 90000–90100 from memory of the prime list).

Terminological inconsistency only: §53–54 count 1 as a prime (26 primes up to 100), while §62 says unity is usually not counted among the primes. This is the period convention, not a mathematical error.
§63 tacitly assumes p ≠ q; Euler repairs this himself on the next page (§64).

results.what: Qualitative statement that primes thin out (decreasing density), with irregular local fluctuations in counts per hundred
results.modern_name: Decreasing prime density; qualitative precursor of the Prime Number Theorem; irregularity of prime counts in short intervals
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore; quantitative density laws to Legendre (1798) and Gauss (c. 1792, published later)

results.modern_name: Values of pi(x+100) - pi(x) from prime tables
results.usually_credited_to: Prime tables of the period (e.g. Krüger, Poetius); Euler citing table data

results.what: Definition of divisor and quotient; 1 and N divide N; divisors of a prime are 1 and p; divisors of pq are 1, p, q, pq

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary textbook material from Euler's known Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792). The only detail of interest is that the prime-century counts, including the sparse hundred 79700–79800 with only 3 primes, are all accurate.

checkable.asserts: the hardest composites in the 79700–79800 sieve
divisors of a product pq of distinct primes are 1, p, q, pq
